# Ang Totoong Narcolist
Ang Totoong Narcolist (Filipino for “The True Narco List”) is a 2019 online video series in the Philippines featuring an anonymous narrator, alias “Bikoy,” who alleged that President Rodrigo Duterte’s family and associates were involved in the illegal drug trade. The videos, released on social media in April 2019, presented documents and code names purportedly showing drug payoffs to Duterte’s son Paolo Duterte, his long-time aide (and future senator) Christopher “Bong” Go, and other individuals. Malacañang (the presidential palace) dismissed the accusations as “black propaganda”, and Bong Go publicly bared his back to prove he did not have the dragon tattoo that the videos claimed was a secret triad identifier linking him to a narcotics syndicate. The videos sparked a political firestorm in the midst of Duterte’s war on drugs and the May 2019 elections. Weeks later, the man behind “Bikoy” surrendered and dramatically retracted his claims, asserting that the narcolist videos were a fabrication orchestrated by opposition figures – a reversal that led to sedition charges against various Duterte critics (later dismissed in court). In 2023, Bikoy (identified as Peter Joemel Advincula) was convicted of perjury for falsely implicating people in the supposed anti-Duterte plot.
## Background and Video Series Content
The emergence of “Ang Totoong Narcolist” came against the backdrop of President Duterte’s campaign against illegal drugs and his public naming of officials allegedly tied to the drug trade. In March 2019, Duterte released a “narco list” of 46 politicians accused of drug links, unprecedentedly exposing local officials purportedly involved in narcotics. Just weeks later, starting on April 2, 2019, a series of anonymously produced videos began circulating on YouTube and Facebook under the title Ang Totoong Narcolist, turning the tables by accusing Duterte’s own relatives and allies of drug involvement. The videos were posted on a channel reportedly associated with a certain “Metro Balita” news page and were released episodically in April 2019, in the run-up to the Philippine midterm elections.
Each episode featured a hooded figure who identified himself by the alias “Bikoy.” Speaking in Tagalog with his face hidden, Bikoy claimed to be a former member of a major drug syndicate operating in Luzon and the Visayas regions. He described his role as a recorder of the cartel’s financial transactions – keeping an internal ledger of narcotics payoffs, known in underworld jargon as “TARA” (an allotted bribe or share). To bolster his allegations, Bikoy showed what he asserted were confidential documents: spreadsheets and bank transaction records of drug money deposits, complete with code names and signatures. According to Bikoy, these documents detailed monthly deposits of drug money to bank accounts of certain “principals” identified by code. He explained that each code corresponded to a real individual, and he pointed to the involvement of figures in Duterte’s inner circle.
In Ang Totoong Narcolist – Episode 1, Bikoy’s narration focused on a person codenamed “POLO DELTA – TSG 01” and “ALPHA TIERRA – 0029,” whom he insinuated was Paolo Duterte (the president’s eldest son). He alleged that tens of millions of pesos in drug money were funneled into bank accounts linked to Paolo Duterte on a monthly basis via intermediaries. Bikoy identified one supposed intermediary as Waldo Carpio, an Agriculture department official who is the brother of Duterte’s son-in-law (Manases Carpio). The narration claimed that in 2018, Waldo Carpio’s account received ₱30 million per month in drug funds, which were then transferred to an account allegedly belonging to Paolo Duterte. Episode 2 continued with further claims, including a mention of another code name “VERA REGA” tied to a certain “Veronica” – a detail that was widely interpreted as alluding to Duterte’s young daughter Veronica “Kitty” Duterte (although the videos did not explicitly name the child). These first two episodes primarily targeted the Duterte family, prompting immediate denials.
Episode 3 of Ang Totoong Narcolist shifted focus to Christopher “Bong” Go, President Duterte’s closest aide and a candidate for senator in 2019. The video accused Go of being linked to the drug syndicate under the code name “TESOROGOLF – TSG 002,” and claimed he had four bank accounts receiving drug payoffs totaling as much as ₱3 billion. Most sensationally, Bikoy alleged that Bong Go bore a tattoo of a dragon on his back containing an alphanumeric code, supposedly proof of his membership in a Chinese triad involved in the narcotics trade. (Go’s own middle name is “Tesoro,” a fact the code name seemed to play on.) This dramatic accusation led Bong Go to respond by publicly exposing his back at campaign rallies and on national television – twice – to show that he had no such tattoo, thereby refuting Bikoy’s claim. Photographs of a tattoo-less Bong Go were widely circulated, and Duterte’s spokesman seized on them as evidence that the narcolist videos were “mere black propaganda”.
Subsequent episodes (Episodes 4 and 5) continued to name alleged players in the supposed drug-money scheme. In these videos, Bikoy implicated other individuals both in and out of government. Notably, in Episode 5, he accused a businessman identified as Elizaldy Co of being a central drug lord heading the syndicate, a claim that prompted at least one legislator allied with Co to call for an investigation into the videos’ dissemination. By the end of the five-part video series (the final episode was released on April 22, 2019), Bikoy had painted an elaborate conspiracy in which Duterte’s family members (including Paolo Duterte) and associates like Bong Go, as well as certain businessmen and lawyers, were raking in proceeds from the illegal drug trade. These explosive allegations, coming amid a heated election season, put the administration on the defensive and led to swift efforts to track down the source of the videos.
## Identification of “Bikoy” and Initial Investigation
As the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos went viral, Philippine authorities moved quickly to investigate their origin. In late April 2019, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) arrested Rodel Jayme, an I.T. professional who was suspected of helping upload or spread the videos online. Jayme was the developer of a website (metrobalita.net) where the videos first appeared. He denied authoring the content, but on May 6, 2019, the Department of Justice filed charges against Rodel Jayme for inciting to sedition in connection with the Bikoy videos. This marked the first official legal action stemming from the video scandal. Jayme later pleaded not guilty, maintaining that he only uploaded content provided to him, but the case signaled the government’s determination to pursue those behind the “Ang Totoong Narcolist” series.
Even as investigators hunted for the mastermind, the mystery of Bikoy’s identity quickly unraveled. On May 6, 2019, the same day charges were announced against Jayme, a man named Peter Joemel Advincula dramatically surfaced at the national headquarters of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) in Pasig City. In a press conference held at the IBP, Advincula announced that he was “Bikoy,” the hooded whistleblower in the videos. Removing his hood, he faced the media and affirmed the veracity of the allegations made in Ang Totoong Narcolist. Advincula provided additional detail about himself: he claimed to have been a former marketing executive of a drug syndicate and said this background gave him direct knowledge of the drug payoffs and bank accounts mentioned in the videos. Notably, he brought documents to the IBP event that he said corroborated the videos’ contents, including what he described as copies of the syndicate’s ledgers.
During this appearance, Advincula also denied any political motivation or backing, portraying himself as a concerned citizen and whistleblower. Speaking partly in Filipino, he insisted, “Wala akong kaugnayan sa kahit sinong kandidato o partido sa politika” (“I have no links to any candidate or political party”), emphasizing that he was not being used by the opposition. At the time, the Duterte administration had hinted that the videos could be part of a broader plot by its critics to discredit the President ahead of the elections. Advincula, however, flatly denied being an agent of any such scheme on May 6. The Integrated Bar of the Philippines, a nationwide lawyers’ association, said Advincula had come to them seeking free legal assistance to sue those he implicated in the drug trade; the IBP declined to represent him, reportedly wary of being politicized in the controversy.
Advincula’s outing of himself as Bikoy made headlines and lent a short-lived credibility boost to the narcolist videos. His story dominated news cycles for a few days, and opposition figures called for the allegations to be investigated rather than dismissed outright. Even Senator Leila de Lima – a detained opposition senator and noted Duterte critic – argued that Bikoy’s claims “should be probed” instead of reflexively labeled as fake, given their gravity. Meanwhile, administration allies continued to assail Advincula’s character. It soon emerged that Peter Joemel Advincula had a criminal past: records showed he had previously been convicted of estafa (financial fraud) and had spent time in prison. This revelation, which Advincula himself acknowledged, raised doubts about his credibility. Duterte’s spokesperson mocked Bikoy as an “ex-convict” peddling lies for money, and the Philippine National Police (PNP) initially indicated skepticism about the veracity of his documents. Nevertheless, at that moment in early May 2019, Advincula was sticking to his story – and the Duterte family was under the shadow of serious accusations.
## Retraction and Allegations of Opposition “Plot”
Just over two weeks after his public appearance at the IBP, Advincula abruptly changed his story. In a stunning turnaround, the man who had stood by the narcolist allegations recanted everything. On May 23, 2019, Advincula surrendered to the Philippine National Police (PNP) and was presented in a press briefing at Camp Crame (the PNP headquarters). Flanked by top police officials, he read out a new sworn statement and issued a public confession: all of the allegations in the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos were “fabricated lies.” Advincula declared that the videos were not a genuine exposé of Duterte’s drug links, but rather a manufactured propaganda plot orchestrated by opposition politicians.
In this press conference, Advincula (Bikoy) claimed that he had been recruited by members of the Liberal Party (LP) and other Duterte critics to create and spread the narcolist videos as part of a scheme to undermine the administration. He specifically accused Senator Antonio Trillanes IV, a prominent opposition figure and vocal Duterte antagonist, of being the mastermind of the video production. He also implicated the camp of Vice President Leni Robredo (the leader of the opposition) and senators aligned with the Liberal Party, such as Senator Risa Hontiveros and former Senator Bam Aquino, as having knowledge of or involvement in the plot. According to Advincula’s new narrative, the elaborate plan was code-named “Project Sodoma.” Its supposed aim was to oust President Duterte from power by spreading scandalous misinformation, thereby boosting the opposition’s chances in the elections and paving the way for Robredo to become President.
Advincula provided a dramatic backstory for how the videos were allegedly concocted. He claimed that starting in August 2018, he was taken in by a group of priests and opposition supporters, and was hidden in a convent in Manila where the videos were later recorded. He alleged that “everything in the videos was scripted” – he was fed lines and fake documents to recite on camera, all under the direction of Trillanes and other conspirators. The hooded outfit and voice distortion in the videos, he said, were meant to conceal that he was acting out a role. Advincula asserted that the true objective of the exercise was to smear administration candidates (particularly Bong Go, who was then running for senator) and “divert the public’s attention” by stirring up outrage against Duterte’s family.
He further explained his motive for coming forward with the supposed truth. Advincula said that after the opposition’s Otso Diretso slate was defeated in the May 13, 2019 elections (none of the opposition’s senatorial candidates won a seat), the plotters abandoned him and he feared for his life. With the Liberal Party’s plan failing and Duterte’s allies victorious, Advincula claimed he was no longer useful to those who enlisted him and that he even suspected they might “silence” him to erase evidence. This, he stated, prompted him to surrender to the police and reveal the scheme before he could be harmed.
The PNP and the Duterte administration heralded Advincula’s retraction as a vindication. Government officials said his new testimony proved that the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos were a “weapon of fake news” used by desperate political enemies. Police quickly pivoted to building a case based on Advincula’s claims of an opposition-led conspiracy. Critics, however, pointed out the extreme turnaround in Advincula’s statements and questioned whether his recantation was credible or made under duress. Media watchdogs and fact-checkers noted inconsistencies in Advincula’s various versions of events. Nonetheless, his May 23 flip-flop had immediate legal repercussions for those he accused.
## Legal Aftermath
### Sedition Complaint and Dismissal
Armed with Advincula’s new affidavit, the PNP’s Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) filed a criminal complaint in July 2019 against numerous opposition figures. The complaint charged over 30 individuals – including Vice President Leni Robredo, Senators Leila de Lima and Risa Hontiveros, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV, several Catholic bishops, lawyers, and members of the Liberal Party – with sedition, inciting to sedition, cyber libel, libel, harboring a criminal, and obstruction of justice, among other offenses. The centerpiece of the complaint was Advincula’s claim that these respondents had conspired to produce the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos as part of “Project Sodoma” to oust Duterte. Essentially, the police accused the opposition of plotting a coup d’etat via propaganda – a charge the accused all vehemently denied.
The Department of Justice convened a panel to evaluate the complaint. In January 2020, after several months of investigation and hearings, the DOJ panel released a resolution partly affirming and partly dismissing the allegations. The DOJ dropped all major charges against most of the respondents, including Vice President Robredo, finding no sufficient evidence of a seditious plot to topple the government. Prosecutors noted that while the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos contained “libelous imputations” against President Duterte and his family that could stir public outrage, they did not find any clear exhortation for the populace to rise up in mass protest or violence. Thus, the element of inciting a rebellion or insurrection (required for sedition) was deemed lacking. All respondents were cleared of the sedition, inciting to sedition, and other complaints like libel and obstruction of justice due to lack of probable cause.
However, the DOJ did move to indict a smaller subset of individuals on a lesser charge. In February 2020, it formally indicted 11 people, including Peter Joemel Advincula himself, for “conspiracy to commit sedition.” Those charged in court comprised Advincula (alias Bikoy), ex-Senator Trillanes, two Catholic priests (Fr. Albert Alejo, SJ and Fr. Flaviano Villanueva), a dismissed police official (Eduardo Acierto), and several noted opposition figures and activists such as Yolanda Ong (a political communications strategist), Vicente Romano III (former tourism official), Jonnell Sangalang, Joel Saracho, “Boom” Enriquez, and a certain alias “Monique”. Notably, Vice President Robredo and most elected opposition politicians were not included in the indictment. The DOJ’s indictment stated that these 11 individuals, acting in concert, had coordinated to spread the Bikoy videos and incite public hatred against Duterte as part of a “grand conspiracy”. The charge of conspiracy to commit sedition under the Revised Penal Code is a felony, but less severe than actual sedition; it essentially alleged that the accused planned to sow unrest even if no uprising occurred.
Those indicted surrendered or voluntarily appeared in court to post bail in early 2020, maintaining their innocence. The case then proceeded to trial at the Quezon City Metropolitan Trial Court. Over the next couple of years, however, the sedition-conspiracy case faltered. The prosecution’s case relied heavily on Advincula’s testimony, yet Advincula did not take the witness stand during the trial. By some accounts, he could not be contacted or was unwilling to repeat his claims under oath in open court. Without Bikoy’s live testimony, the remaining evidence (such as gadget receipts and meeting photos presented by the DOJ) was largely circumstantial. In September 2023, the court dismissed the conspiracy to commit sedition case against Trillanes, Advincula, and all the other accused due to insufficient evidence. In its ruling, the court noted that the prosecution failed to prove that any of the accused had actually conspired to spread the videos to incite sedition. It emphasized that much of the government’s case was hearsay without Advincula’s direct verification in court. The judge concluded that there was no way to establish the truth of Advincula’s allegations if he himself did not substantiate them under oath, and thus a guilty verdict could not be supported. All of the accused were accordingly acquitted or cleared, and the sedition plot case was put to rest.
### Perjury Conviction of Advincula (Bikoy)
Even as the sedition case against the opposition unraveled, Peter Joemel Advincula (Bikoy) faced his own legal troubles for the conflicting stories he had told. In July 2019, when Advincula submitted his sworn statements accusing various opposition members (the Project Sodoma affidavit), he directly implicated three human rights lawyers – Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno, Theodore Te, and Erin Tañada III – as alleged co-conspirators who masterminded or facilitated the Bikoy videos. These three lawyers, all respected figures and coincidentally opposition-aligned (they were part of the Free Legal Assistance Group and two had run as opposition senatorial candidates), vehemently denied Advincula’s accusations. After the DOJ cleared them of the sedition complaint in early 2020, Diokno, Te, and Tañada turned the tables on Advincula by filing a perjury case against him. They asserted that Advincula willfully lied in his affidavits, falsely implicating them in a crime, which is a criminal offense (perjury) since those statements were made under oath.
The perjury case went to trial in Manila. Advincula was accused of making false testimonies in his July 2019 sworn statement – specifically, the lie that Diokno, Te, and Tañada had met with him at Ateneo de Manila University on a certain date to plan ousting Duterte. (In reality, the lawyers were attending an election forum at Ateneo and said they never met Advincula there, as confirmed by event records.) During the trial, evidence showed that Advincula’s assertions were untrue, and the court noted that the DOJ itself had earlier observed that Advincula was probably the one committing falsehoods about the supposed conspiracy.
On May 24, 2023, the Metropolitan Trial Court of Manila found Peter Joemel Advincula guilty of perjury beyond reasonable doubt. In its decision, the court cited the “falsehood” of Advincula’s claims against the three lawyers and stressed that his sworn statements were refuted by solid evidence. Advincula was sentenced to a minimum of 3 months and 1 day to a maximum of 1 year and 1 day in prison for the offense. The conviction effectively affirmed that his allegations of an opposition plot were lies. Advincula’s camp indicated he would appeal the verdict, but the judgment was hailed by the falsely accused individuals as a measure of justice. It also cast a definitive cloud over the veracity of the original Ang Totoong Narcolist claims.

Nonetheless, Advincula's May 23 flip-flop had immediate legal repercussions for those he accused.
Armed with Advincula’s new affidavit, the PNP’s Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) filed a criminal complaint in July 2019 against numerous opposition figures.

The complaint charged over 30 individuals – including Vice President Leni Robredo, Senators Leila de Lima and Risa Hontiveros, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV, several Catholic bishops, lawyers, and members of the Liberal Party – with sedition, inciting to sedition, cyber libel, libel, harboring a criminal, and obstruction of justice, among other offenses.
The centerpiece of the complaint was Advincula’s claim that these respondents had conspired to produce the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos as part of “Project Sodoma” to oust Duterte.
Essentially, the police accused the opposition of plotting a coup d’etat via propaganda – a charge the accused all vehemently denied.
The Department of Justice convened a panel to evaluate the complaint.
In January 2020, after several months of investigation and hearings, the DOJ panel released a resolution partly affirming and partly dismissing the allegations.
The DOJ dropped all major charges against most of the respondents, including Vice President Robredo, finding no sufficient evidence of a seditious plot to topple the government.

Prosecutors noted that while the Ang Totoong Narcolist videos contained “libelous imputations” against President Duterte and his family that could stir public outrage, they did not find any clear exhortation for the populace to rise up in mass protest or violence.
Thus, the element of inciting a rebellion or insurrection (required for sedition) was deemed lacking.
All respondents were cleared of the sedition, inciting to sedition, and other complaints like libel and obstruction of justice due to lack of probable cause.
However, the DOJ did move to indict a smaller subset of individuals on a lesser charge.
In February 2020, the DOJ formally indicted 11 people, including Peter Joemel Advincula himself, for “conspiracy to commit sedition.”

Those charged in court comprised Advincula (alias Bikoy), ex-Senator Trillanes, two Catholic priests (Fr. Albert Alejo, SJ and Fr. Flaviano Villanueva), a dismissed police official (Eduardo Acierto), and several noted opposition figures and activists such as Yolanda Ong (a political communications strategist), Vicente Romano III (former tourism official), Jonnell Sangalang, Joel Saracho, “Boom” Enriquez, and a certain alias “Monique”.
Notably, Vice President Robredo and most elected opposition politicians were not included in the indictment.
The DOJ’s indictment stated that these 11 individuals, acting in concert, had coordinated to spread the Bikoy videos and incite public hatred against Duterte as part of a “grand conspiracy”.
The charge of conspiracy to commit sedition under the Revised Penal Code is a felony, but less severe than actual sedition.
The charge of conspiracy to commit sedition essentially alleged that the accused planned to sow unrest even if no uprising occurred.
Those indicted surrendered or voluntarily appeared in court to post bail in early 2020, maintaining their innocence.
The case then proceeded to trial at the Quezon City Metropolitan Trial Court.
Over the next couple of years, however, the sedition-conspiracy case faltered.
The prosecution’s case relied heavily on Advincula’s testimony, yet Advincula did not take the witness stand during the trial.
By some accounts, Advincula could not be contacted or was unwilling to repeat his claims under oath in open court.
Without Bikoy’s live testimony, the remaining evidence (such as gadget receipts and meeting photos presented by the DOJ) was largely circumstantial.
In September 2023, the court dismissed the conspiracy to commit sedition case against Trillanes, Advincula, and all the other accused due to insufficient evidence.
In its ruling, the court noted that the prosecution failed to prove that any of the accused had actually conspired to spread the videos to incite sedition.
The court emphasized that much of the government’s case was hearsay without Advincula’s direct verification in court.
The judge concluded that there was no way to establish the truth of Advincula’s allegations if he himself did not substantiate them under oath, and thus a guilty verdict could not be supported.
All of the accused were accordingly acquitted or cleared, and the sedition plot case was put to rest.
Even as the sedition case against the opposition unraveled, Peter Joemel Advincula (Bikoy) faced his own legal troubles for the conflicting stories he had told.

In July 2019, when Advincula submitted his sworn statements accusing various opposition members (the Project Sodoma affidavit), he directly implicated three human rights lawyers – Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno, Theodore Te, and Erin Tañada III – as alleged co-conspirators who masterminded or facilitated the Bikoy videos.

These three lawyers, all respected figures and coincidentally opposition-aligned (they were part of the Free Legal Assistance Group and two had run as opposition senatorial candidates), vehemently denied Advincula’s accusations.
After the DOJ cleared them of the sedition complaint in early 2020, Diokno, Te, and Tañada turned the tables on Advincula by filing a perjury case against him.
They asserted that Advincula willfully lied in his affidavits, falsely implicating them in a crime, which is a criminal offense (perjury) since those statements were made under oath.
The perjury case went to trial in Manila.

Advincula was accused of making false testimonies in his July 2019 sworn statement – specifically, the lie that Diokno, Te, and Tañada had met with him at Ateneo de Manila University on a certain date to plan ousting Duterte.
In reality, the lawyers were attending an election forum at Ateneo and said they never met Advincula there, as confirmed by event records.

During the trial, evidence showed that Advincula’s assertions were untrue, and the court noted that the DOJ itself had earlier observed that Advincula was probably the one committing falsehoods about the supposed conspiracy.
On May 24, 2023, the Metropolitan Trial Court of Manila found Peter Joemel Advincula guilty of perjury beyond reasonable doubt.
In its decision, the court cited the “falsehood” of Advincula’s claims against the three lawyers and stressed that his sworn statements were refuted by solid evidence.
Advincula was sentenced to a minimum of 3 months and 1 day to a maximum of 1 year and 1 day in prison for the offense.
The conviction effectively affirmed that Advincula's allegations of an opposition plot were lies.
Advincula’s camp indicated he would appeal the verdict, but the judgment was hailed by the falsely accused individuals as a measure of justice.
The judgment also cast a definitive cloud over the veracity of the original Ang Totoong Narcolist claims.

DOJ clears Robredo, indicts Trillanes and 10 others for 'conspiracy to commit sedition'
=======================================================================================

By NICOLE-ANNE C. LAGRIMAS, GMA News

**Published** February 10, 2020 1:39pm  
**Updated** February 10, 2020 2:12pm

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has cleared Vice President Leni Robredo and several opposition figures of sedition but indicted former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV and 10 others for "conspiracy to commit sedition" over an alleged ouster plot against President Rodrigo Duterte.

Prosecutors indicted Trillanes, Peter Joemel Advincula alias "Bikoy," dismissed police official Eduardo Acierto, and Fr. Albert Alejo for conspiracy to commit sedition under Article 141 of the Revised Penal Code, the DOJ said Monday.

Jonnel Sangalang, Yolanda Villuaneva Ong, Fr. Flaviano Villanueva, Vicente Romano III, Joel Saracho, Boom Enriquez, and one alias "Monique" were also indicted.

Robredo, Senators Risa Hontiveros and Leila de Lima, former Senator Bam Aquino, members of the Otso Diretso senatorial slate, lawyers, and some Catholic bishops were not included in the indictment.

"All respondents," meanwhile, were cleared of sedition, inciting to sedition, cyberlibel, libel, estafa and obstruction of justice for lack of probable cause

"In finding no probable cause for sedition or inciting to sedition, the Panel found the element of public and tumultuous uprising wanting," the DOJ said in a statement.

"It further explained that while the video series 'contains libelous imputations against President Duterte and his family which tend to create hatred or revenge against them,' nonetheless no words were uttered which tended to incite the people to take up arms or rise against the government," the DOJ added.

The Philippine National Police's Criminal Investigation and Detection Group had filed a complaint against the respondents for those charges based on allegations by Advincula that they were involved in "Project Sodoma," an alleged plot to unseat Duterte and install Robredo in his place.

Advincula, an estafa convict, alleged that the "Ang Totoong Narcolist" videos, a series of videos implicating Duterte, his family, and Senator Bong Go in the illegal drug trade, were part of Project Sodoma.

Advincula claims to be Bikoy, the hooded figure who narrated the videos. He is both a respondent and a witness in the sedition complaint.

He surfaced at the Integrated Bar of the Philippines' (IBP) headquarters last May 2019 to stand by the allegations made in the videos, only to surrender to the police weeks later to tag the Liberal Party as the mastermind of the series.

The IBP denied his request for legal aid. He eventually came to be represented by Lorenzo Gadon, the lawyer who filed the petition that led to then-chief justice Maria Lourdes Sereno's ouster in 2018 and lost in the senatorial elections the following year.

**'Grand conspiracy'**

The panel of prosecutors said the indictment was based on evidence that showed a "complete picture of the grand conspiracy between and among some respondents to create hatred or revenge against the President and his family with the end in view of toppling and destabilizing the current administration."

These "interlocking pieces of proof" are the online publication of the Bikoy videos, the press conference that Advincula held when he surfaced at the IBP, Acierto's press statement accusing Duterte of drug links, and "admissions" by the respondents, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said the panel found that the Bikoy videos were made by Advincula, Saracho, Enriquez, alias "Monique," Ong, and Romano, and that Alejo prepared the Jesuit Communications at the Ateneo De Manila University where the videos were allegedly taken.

Apart from Advincula's word, the panel considered the following as evidence: USB drives, photos of the respondents, keys and access cards of the places Advincula and his companions stayed, utility bills and receipts, and purchase receipts of gadgets and electronic devices allegedly used in producing the videos.

**'Absurd case'**

In a statement, Trillanes called the new charge — as well as the government's filing of a quo warranto petition against ABS-CBN — the "latest absurd case."

"This latest absurd case is but another proof that the Duterte administration continues to weaponize the law against the political opposition, critics and the media," he said.

"But let me assure Mr. Duterte that we will not be cowed by such political persecution. On the contrary, we are more determined and motivated to continue our fight for democracy and the rights of our people," he added.

The former senator also faces a revived rebellion case over the 2007 Manila Peninsula Siege. His trial will resume in April. —**KBK, GMA News**

![Image 1](https://verafiles.org/wp-content/uploads/3015/54/BikoyVF-1.jpg)

This is a classic case of Duterte getting a dose of his own medicine.

Two weeks after he released the initial list of local officials allegedly involved in drug trafficking, two videos implicating the President’s son, former Davao City Vice Mayor Paolo Duterte and now candidate for Representative of Davao City’s first district, were uploaded onYou Tube and Facebook account of “Metro Balita”, which lists itself as “media/news company.”

Titled “Ang Totoong Narcolist” , Episode 1 is 6 minutes and 50 seconds long. Episode 2 is three minutes and 30 seconds.

The videos look professionally done. So is the annotation.

The video shows a hooded whistleblower, who identified himself as “Bikoy”- not his real name, -who claims to be a former member of a drug syndicate operating in Southern Luzon and Visayas region. He said he was involved in the recording of transactions which explains the documents that he presented in the video.

He said his work involved recording how much money is allotted per leader of the syndicate monthly.

![Image 2](https://verafiles.org/wp-content/uploads/5415/54/Alpha_tierraVF-1.jpg)

The documents, the narrator said, were the syndicate’s internal documents referred to as TARA since 2010. A typical TARA document has a date, the code name of the principal, the bank accounts of the principal and the deposits made. At the bottom of the documents are signature which the narrator said were to proof that the listed details in the documents are accurate.

The principal of one document Bikoy presented has two codenames. One wasPOLO DELTA-TSG01 and the other was ALPHA TIERRA-0029.

The narrator commented the principal was not “so bright” because his code name was close to his real name.

According to the document, the account of Principal number one was in the name of Carpio Reyes Waldo and Carpio Waldo.

Waldo Carpio is the brother of Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, who was mentioned in last year’s scandal of the P6 billion shabu smuggling allegedly facilitated by the Davao Group.

Waldo Carpio is agriculture undersecretary.

![Image 3](https://verafiles.org/wp-content/uploads/3415/54/Signatures_VF-1.jpg)

In the 2018 summary of deposits of Waldo Carpio’s account, the monthly deposit was P30 million. Then the money were transferred to another account which the annotator said belonged to Paolo Duterte.

Malacañang immediately dismissed it as “black propaganda.” The Philippine National Police won’t dare touch the subject.

Paolo Duterte’s reaction?

In his Facebook account, the next representative of Davao’s first district said ranted without refuting the details Bikoy showed like the bank accounts. Paolo merely said:

“Wow ha kung makaimbento ka wagas. Galit ka kay Waldo kasi binabara niya lahat ng smuggling mo ng bigas at asukal diba J.S. (Wow, you’re so good at inventing. You’re mad at Waldo because he is blocking your rice and sugar smuggling. Right J.S?).

“Galit ka sa akin kasi di kita pinansin sa eroplano kasi hambog ka! Ngayon pansinin na kita kasama ng kamay ko na kasing laki ng mukha mo pag nangyari yan. Yan ang totoong balita (You’re mad at me because I snubbed you on a flight because you’re so arrogant. Now, I’m giving you attention – with my hand as big as your face. That’s real news).”

And Sara Duterte?

She skipped the Hugpong rally at Tangub. Misamis Occidental Wednesday. At first the reports said to attend to a “family matter” that is an “emergency. “ The next day, reports said it was due to “security.”

That was a few hours after Episode 2 of “AngTotoong Narcolist” was uploaded. It mentioned a codename VERA REGA and identified a recipient: Veronica Salvador.

This is riveting.

Advincula: ‘Walang dragon tattoo si Bong Go’
============================================

By [ANNA FELICIA BAJO](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/archives/authors/annafeliciabajo/)

**Published** May 23, 2019 10:55am  
**Updated** May 23, 2019 11:00am

Peter Joemel Advincula, the man who claimed to be "Bikoy" in the series of anti-Duterte videos, on Thursday said Senator-elect Christopher "Bong" Go has no dragon tattoo.

"Hindi totoo. Walang dragon tattoo si Bong Go. Kaya nga nung lumitaw sa Episode 3 na may dragon tattoo si Bong Go, naghanap na naman kami ng paraan para palitawin na talagang may tattoo siya," Advincula said at a press conference in Camp Crame.

Advincula, meanwhile, said he had no idea if former Davao City Vice Mayor incoming Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte has tattoo on his back.

"Kay Paolo, hindi ko alam kung talagang may tattoo..." he said.

In a video titled "Ang Totoong Narco List - Episode 3,” the narrator accused Go of owning four local bank accounts and receiving drug money payoffs as much as P3 billion, then using them as campaign funds for the 2019 elections.

The narrator said Go, who supposedly uses the code name "TESOROGOLF-TSG-002," has a dragon tattoo on his back.

During his press conference at the office of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) on May 6, Advincula said he had scanned the dragon tattoo on Go's back.

“Ilang beses din na ako mismo ang nag-iiscan ng code sa likod ni Bong Go kaya tinitiyak ko po sa inyo na may dragon tattoo siya pati na rin si Paolo Duterte," Advincula said.

Go has since shown his back twice to belie accusations that he has a tattoo with a supposed code linking him to illegal drug trade.

Advincula said the "Ang Totoong Narcolist" videos were all lies as these videos only aim to discredit the Duterte administration. **— RSJ, GMA News**

In a 180-degree turn, Peter Joemel Advincula who claims to be “Bikoy,” the hooded man in the “Ang Totoong Narco List” videos, now implicated the Liberal Party (LP) and Sen. Antonio Trillanes in the video series that linked members of the president’s family and his allies to the illegal drug trade.

From categorically stating he was “not connected” to any political party or affiliation, Advincula changed his story after being taken under police custody 17 days since his press briefing at the Integrated Bar of the Philippines.

**STATEMENT**

In a press briefing at the Philippine National Police, May 23, a day after he supposedly surrendered to authorities, Advincula said of the claims made in the video series:

> _“Hindi totoo ‘yun. Walang katotohanan lahat-lahat ‘yun_ (They’re not true. There’s no truth to all of those)_. At ‘yoon pawang_ orchestrated _lamang ng mga nasa kabilang_ party (And \[those claims\] were only orchestrated by those in the opposition party)_,_ which is the Liberal Party under the handling of Senator Antonio “Sonny” Trillanes IV.”
> 
> Source: PNP official Facebook page, NOW: Media briefing on the surrender of Peter Joemel Advincula, the confessed “Bikoy” character behind the “Ang Totoong Narcolist” video series, May 23, 2019, [watch](https://www.facebook.com/pnp.pio/videos/618971635248454/?t=446) from 7:28 to 7:47

**FLIP-FLOP**

This is the exact opposite of what Advincula said during a May 6 press briefing at the IBP, the first time he claimed he was Bikoy in the video series:

> “_Gusto kong linawin na wala akong kaugnayan sa kahit kaninong kandidato. Lalo na sa mga kandidato ng Otso Diretso, o anumang_ political party _o_ political affiliation.  
> (I just want to clarify that I have no connection to any of the candidates. Especially to those of Otso Diretso, or any political party or affiliation.)”
> 
> Source: ABS-CBN, Man behind viral anti-Duterte video surfaces, May 6, 2019, [watch](https://youtu.be/MX_zHFD5pgk?t=65) from 1:05 to 1:20

But in a May 23 statement, he insisted that he did not know Rodel Jayme, who was charged with inciting to sedition for allegedly uploading and sharing the controversial videos. Advincula also said he was not connected to and had “never even met” the media personalities in Malaca[ñ](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%C3%B1)ang’s matrix on the supposed destabilization plot against the government.

This is consistent with his statement where he said he had “no connection” to media personalities and institutions named in the matrix presented by Malaca[ñ](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%C3%B1)ang. The matrix, using the “Ang Totoong Narcolist” videos, lumped together some journalists, lawyers, and opposition figures in an alleged destabilization plot against the government.

A QUEZON City court has junked a case of conspiracy to commit sedition against former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, Peter Joemel “Bikoy” Advincula and several others in relation to an alleged plot to unseat former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Quezon City Metropolitan Trial Court Branch 138 dismissed the case as it approved the demurrer to evidence filed separately by Trillanes, Advincula, Jonnel Sangalang, Yolanda Villanueva Ong, Fr. Flaviano Villanueva, Fr. Albert Elejo, Vicente Romano III, and Ronnil Carlo Enriquez.

It said the prosecution failed to present competent or sufficient evidence to sustain the indictment or support a verdict of guilt against the accused.

"Succinctly, the prosecution failed to prove the commission of the crime of conspiracy to commit sedition as alleged in the information and the precise degree of participation therein by all accused," the resolution stated.

"Basic is the rule in evidence that a witness can testify only on the facts that he knows from his own personal knowledge or those that are derived from his perception…A witness may not testify on what he merely learned, read, or heard from others because such testimony is considered hearsay and may not be received as proof of the truth of what he has learned, read, or heard," it added.

It was also noted that Advincula was not presented during the trial, which is vital to support his sworn statements on his claims.

Advincula was the person in a series of viral videos entitled “Ang Totoong Narco-list” released in 2019 where he linked Duterte, as well as the members of his family to the illegal drugs trade.

As he surrendered, Advincula tagged several personalities under the Liberal Party to be behind “Project Sodoma,” which includes the series of videos that aims to oust Duterte and put then Vice President Leni Robredo in power.

In May, a Manila court found Advincula guilty of perjury, a case filed against him by Free Legal Assistance Group (Flag) lawyers Chel Diokno, Erin Tañada and Theodore Te.

Advincula tagged the three lawyers as the brains behind Project Sodoma. He later retracted his claims. **(SunStar Philippines)**

No dragon tattoo: Go bares back in Agusan
=========================================

[Philippine Daily Inquirer](https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/source/philippine-daily-inquirer) / 05:14 AM April 11, 2019

Share:

[![Image 24: Copy Link](https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/single2017/images/copy-link.svg)](https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1105496/no-dragon-tattoo-go-bares-back-in-agusan#)

[![Image 26: Bookmark](blob:https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/76f70cba1a4985ff842bd808acca549c)](https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1105496/no-dragon-tattoo-go-bares-back-in-agusan#)

![Image 32](https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/files/2019/04/20190410_Bong-Go-bares-back2.jpg)Look: Bong Go got no dragon tattoo. Photo from Bong Go

DAVAO CITY — Look, no tattoo.

Senatorial candidate and former Special Assistant to the President Christopher “Bong” Go on Wednesday took off his shirt at a campaign rally here to belie claims that he had a tattoo supposedly containing his code name as a member of a drug syndicate.

_Article continues after this advertisement_

In episode 3 of the video “The Real Narcolist (Ang Totoong Narcolist),” which has been making the rounds of social media since last week, “Bikoy” — a man claiming to be a former drug syndicate member — alleged that Go received about P3 billion in drug money from the syndicate from 2010 to 2018.

He also said that Go used the code name “Tesorogolf-TSG-002,” which is supposedly tattooed on his back. Go’s middle name is Tesoro.

**‘End all this talk’**

“Let’s put an end to all this talk,” Go said, showing his bare back to reporters at a press conference in Prosperidad town, Agusan del Sur, where the administration-backed Hugpong ng Pagbabago held a campaign rally.

“Is it clear? This is my mark,” Go said, pointing to the number 34 emblazoned on the back of the red polo shirt he changed into after taking off his white shirt.

_Article continues after this advertisement_

Go said he suspected that Bikoy was a drug lord.

The hooded figure in the video made similar claims against President Rodrigo Duterte’s son, Paolo, the former Davao City vice mayor, in episode 1 of the video, and implicated the President’s partner Honeylet Avanceña and their daughter, Veronica, in episode 2.

_Article continues after this advertisement_

Paolo Duterte has refused to show his back and instead challenged his critics to get their own tattoo.

**‘Black propaganda’**

Reacting to Go’s stunt, presidential spokesperson Salvador Panelo said Malacañang had been “saying all along that (the video) is black propaganda.”

“There are people who believe it, hook, line and sinker. It’s now \[been shown\] that it’s not true. It’s never been true,” he said.

Asked what he would say to the President’s critics whom he had accused of being behind the videos, Panelo said: “None. They can do their worst, we will do our best.”

On whether Go’s action would affect Bikoy’s other allegations in the video, Panelo said the accusers should provide clear evidence.

==================================================================

\- [INQUIRER.net](https://bandera.inquirer.net/source/inquirer-net-2) May 23, 2019 - 05:03 PM  

![Image 7](https://bandera.inquirer.net/files/2019/05/advincula-bikoy-pnp-1024x768.jpeg)

KUMAMBYO ang nagpakilala na “Bikoy” na naunang naglabas ng mga video ng “Ang Totoong Narcolist” at nagdawit sa droga sa pamilya at kaalyado ni Pangulong Duterte.

Sa isang press conference, sinabi ni Peter Joemel Advincula alyas Bikoy na gawa-gawa lamang ang kanyang mga alegasyon.

“Ang lahat ng nangyari sa ‘Ang Totoong Narcolist’ video episode 1 to video episode 5, ‘yong nirecord ko no’ng nasa isang kumbento ako, lahat ‘yon pawang scripted, lahat ‘yon pawang kasinungalingan,” sabi ni Bikoy, na nasa kustodiya na ng Philippine National Police (PNP).

Sinabi ni Bikoy na layunin lamang ng mga video na siraan ang mga kandidato ng administrasyon, kabilan na si Special Assistant to the President (SAP) and now senator-elect Christopher “Bong” Go.

Inakusahan niya ang mga miyembro ng Liberal Party (LP), kabilang sina Sen. Risa Hontiveros, Sen. Leila de Lima, at Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV na siyang nasa likod ng paglalabas ng mga video.

“Kasinungalingan kasi may plano ‘yong kabilang kampo, ‘yong kabilang kampo magpaputok ng issue para ma-divert ‘yong attention ng tao, papataas nang papataas ang ratings ng administration candidate samantalang walang pumapasok particularly sa Otso Diretso candidate,” ayon pa kay Bikoy.

“At ito nga ‘yong paputok nong kay Bikoy, para ma-discredit si Senator-elect Bong Go \[…\] hindi totoo ‘yon, walang katotothana lahat lahat ‘yon, at ‘yon pawang orchestrated lamang ng mga nasa-kabilang party which is the Liberal Party under the handling of Senator Antonio Trillanes IV,” sabi pa ni Advincula.

Sinabi pa ni Advincula na lumabas siya dahil sa umano’y banta sa kanyang buhay matapos umanong matalo ang buong Otso Diretso sa 2019 midterm elections.

“Hindi ko ho kaya na panindigan ‘yong mga scripted lang ng kwento na ngayong talo na ‘yong mga kandidato nila nararamdaman ko unti-unti na akong nilalaglag, at ang kinakatakutan ko ay baka sila pa ang mag-eliminate sa akin kalaunan dahil wala na akong silbi,” ayon pa kay Advincula.

‘Bikoy’ guilty of perjury, faces up to 3 years in jail
======================================================

![Image 7](https://cdn.manilastandard.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/33dc9_bikoy_thumbnail.jpg)

A Manila court has found whistleblower Peter Joemel Advincula, who goes by the alias “Bikoy,” guilty of perjury in connection with claims he made against three lawyers in 2019.

The Manila Metropolitan Trial Court Branch 17 sentenced Advincula to an indeterminate penalty of three months and one day to one year and one day of imprisonment.

\- Advertisement - 

The case stemmed from the complaint of Jose Manuel Diokno, Theodore Te, and Lorenzo Tañada III in connection with a sworn statement Bikoy submitted on July 18, 2019 before prosecutors alleging that the three civil rights lawyers were part of a group known as “Project Sodoma.”

The group, Advincula claimed, plotted to commit sedition, libel, and cyber libel, among others.

Bikoy also claimed there was a meeting at the Ateneo de Manila University among the conspirators.

Diokno and Tañada said their presence at Ateneo was to attend a forum for senatorial candidates. They also denied meeting Advincula.

The statements became the basis for charges of sedition filed against members of the opposition, including the lawyers, at that time.

The criminal charges, however, were dismissed by the Department of Justice on January 27, 2020, with prosecutors noting that it was Advincula who was probably guilty of the crime of conspiracy to commit sedition.

“In this case, the totality of the prosecution evidence, when put under severe testing, amounts to proof beyond reasonable doubt of the crime of perjury. The witnesses who testified for the prosecution were able to sufficiently establish the falsehood of the accused’s statements,” the court said.
